lines.cap: **Narrator:** Queenstown. Six-thirty p.m. Mei is texting the family group chat about dinner.
**Mei:** Sent! '**Let's eat Grandma!**'
**Ah Ma:** Excuse me?! I cook curry chicken for twelve years and now you want to **eat** your grandmother?!
**Kevin:** You forgot me! Without a **comma of direct address**, 'Grandma' is the **object** of 'eat'! You've made dinner a crime!
**Narrator:** Wednesday. Room 8H. Mr Hargreaves has finally reached mug twenty-three out of twenty-three.
**Full Stop:** Full Stop. Kevin called backup. Sentence. Over.
**Semicolon:** Semicolon; Kevin's older cousin. I hold two main clauses together without breaking a sweat.
**Apostrophe:** And I'm Apostrophe! Another hawker stall wrote **FRIED NOODLE'S** with an apostrophe and I haven't slept since Tuesday!
**Mr H:** Last episode of the year, 8H. Grammar, punctuation and vocabulary.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode sixteen: Let's Eat, Grandma.
**Mr H:** Lewis Carroll wrote: ''Twas brillig, and the **slithy toves** did **gyre** in the wabe.' Nonsense words — yet you know their **word classes**.
**Mei:** Because of their **jobs**! '**Toves**' follows 'the', so it's a **noun**; '**slithy**' describes it — **adjective**; '**gyre**' follows 'did' — **verb**!
**Nib:** Know all eight! **Nouns** include **proper** capitals like Singapore and **abstract nouns** for untouchable ideas like courage.
**Mr H:** **Verbs** include **modals** of possibility and obligation: **can, could, might, must, should**.
**Will:** Careful with '-ly': most are **adverbs**, like 'quickly', yet '**friendly**', '**lovely**' and my beloved '**lonely**' are **adjectives**!
**Nib:** **Earliest recorded user** of 'lonely', Will. Still not its inventor.

**Nib:** Spot the job: in '**my** bag', 'my' is a **determiner** before a noun; in 'the bag is **mine**', 'mine' stands alone as a **pronoun**. **Prepositions** show position: **under, through, beside**.
**Mr H:** Unlock unfamiliar vocabulary with **roots**: Greek **chron** means time, Latin **bene** means good and **mal** means bad — so **malevolent** means wishing harm.
**Kevin:** And for **affect** versus **effect**, use **RAVEN**: **R**emember, **A**ffect is a **V**erb, **E**ffect is a **N**oun! Just like British **practise** with an 's' for the verb!

chapters.title: Phrases, clauses and four sentence types

lines.cap: **Mr H:** A **phrase** has no subject doing a verb: 'under the old bridge'. A **clause** has a **subject** and a **verb**: 'the river froze'.
**Full Stop:** 'The river froze.' **Main clause**. Stands alone. Sentence. Over.

**Nib:** Add a **subordinating conjunction** — **AAAWWUBBIS**: **After, Although, As, When, While, Until, Before, Because, If, Since** — and it becomes a **subordinate clause** that cannot stand alone.
**Kevin:** And when that subordinate clause comes **first** — '**Although** she was terrified**,** Lina stepped forward' — put me right after it!
**Nib:** A **relative clause** starts with **who, which, that** or **whose** to describe a noun: 'the lift, **which had been humming**, stopped'.
**Mr H:** Sentence types depend on **clauses**, not length! Twenty words with **one** main clause is still a **simple sentence**.
**Semicolon:** Join two equal main clauses with **FANBOYS** — **For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So** — or with me, and you have a **compound sentence**.
**Will:** George Orwell opens **Nineteen Eighty-Four** with a compound jolt: 'It was a bright cold day in April, **and** the clocks were striking **thirteen**.'
**Mei:** Main plus subordinate is **complex**; and no main verb at all — like '**Darkness.**' — is a **minor sentence** for impact!
**Mei:** Look at my sentence: 'The match was cancelled, it had rained all night.' I paused for breath, so I used Kevin!
**Kevin:** PAPER BAG! PAPER BAG! Those are **two main clauses**! I'm a comma, not structural concrete! That's a **comma splice**!
**Full Stop:** Three legal fixes. Fix one: use me. 'The match was cancelled**.** It had rained all night.'

**Semicolon:** Fix two: use a **semicolon** to balance two closely linked clauses: 'The match was cancelled**;** it had rained all night.' Venetian printer Aldus Manutius invented me in the **1490s**.
**Mr H:** Fix three: add a conjunction like '**because**'. And watch the biggest exam trap: '**however**' and '**therefore**' are **adverbs**, NOT conjunctions!
**Semicolon:** Never write ', however,'. Put **me** or Full Stop in front: 'I was tired**; however,** I kept going.'
**Will:** Charles Dickens spliced on purpose in **A Tale of Two Cities** — 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' — for breathless antithesis. Do **not** try that in an essay.
**Kevin:** Use me for **lists** — a missing Oxford comma cost a dairy company **five million dollars** in **2017**! — and around removable **non-defining** clauses!
**Nib:** A **colon** needs a **complete main clause** before it, then points like a drumroll to a list, explanation or reveal: 'The plan was simple**:** wait, slip past, and run.'
**Mr H:** **Dashes** add a dramatic twist; **brackets** whisper a quiet aside; and a shorter **hyphen** joins words like '**well-known**'.
**Apostrophe:** Listen carefully, Year 8! I have **only two jobs** in the English language! **Never** use me to make a plural! Just write **bananas** and **the 1990s**!
**Apostrophe:** Job one: **omission** — showing missing letters, like **don't**, **they're**, and **it's** meaning **it is**.
**Mr H:** Job two: **possession**. Singular owner: **the girl's bag**. Plural already ending in 's': after the 's' — **the girls' changing room**.
**Mei:** What about '**children**'? It's already plural without an 's' — so we add apostrophe 's': **the children's toys**!
**Apostrophe:** And **possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe**: **its, hers, yours, theirs, whose**! The dog wagged **its** tail — no apostrophe!
**Nib:** Test your **homophones**: **they're** means they are, **their** shows belonging, **there** is a place. **Who's** is who is; **whose** shows belonging.
**Kevin:** In **dialogue**, put me **inside** the closing speech marks before a reporting clause: '"I'm cold**,**" she said.'
**Mr H:** And start a **new line for every new speaker** — part of **TiPToP**: **Time, Place, Topic, Person**.

chapters.title: Standard English, register and Kevin's moment

lines.cap: **Mei:** Quick proofread! 'Me and Arjun was late, we could of ran faster.'
**Mr H:** Four fixes: subject '**Arjun and I**', plural '**were**', semicolon for the splice, and '**could have** run' — never 'could of'!
**Nib:** Match the **true subject**: 'The **box** of chocolates **was** full', and '**Each** of the players **receives** a medal.'
**Mr H:** **Active voice**: 'The dog bit the postman.' **Passive voice** uses **be** plus past participle — 'Mistakes **were made**' — shifting focus or hiding the blame!

**Nib:** Match **register** to audience. **Singlish** words like **kiasu** and **shiok** are in the Oxford English Dictionary — brilliant with friends, while **code-switching** to formal **Standard English** wins exam marks.
**Mei:** And in essays, we analyse grammar with **PEEL**: Dickens's parallel clauses in '**best of times, worst of times**' create breathless **antithesis**, linking to a world torn by revolution!
**Narrator:** Friday, seven p.m. Queenstown. Mei picks up her phone one more time.
**Mei:** Kevin — right here, after 'eat'. '**Let's eat, Grandma!**'
**Kevin:** Direct address! Grammatically necessary! Nobody gets eaten! Best day of my life!
**Ah Ma:** Much better! Come and eat — I fried twenty-three curry puffs!
**Narrator:** End of the school year. One last round of mark-savers from Room 8H.
**Mei:** Memory hooks! Compound clauses: **FANBOYS**. Subordinate clauses: **AAAWWUBBIS**. Paragraphs: **TiPToP**. Affect verb, effect noun: **RAVEN**!
**Kevin:** One. Never **comma-splice** two main clauses! Fix with a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction.
**Semicolon:** Two. '**However**' and '**therefore**' are adverbs — put a **semicolon** or **full stop** before them, never just a comma.
**Apostrophe:** Three. **Its** without an apostrophe shows belonging; **it's** means it is. And **never** use an apostrophe for plurals!
**Mr H:** Four. Write **could have**, never 'could of', keep **one tense**, and match verbs to the **true subject**.
**Nib:** Five. Keep speech punctuation **inside** closing speech marks, start a **new line per speaker**, and use formal **Standard English** in exams.
**Full Stop:** Six. Simple sentences can be long; minor sentences have no main verb. Choose each for **effect**. Sentence. Over.
**Mei:** Final Year 8 reviews! Will: **four and a half stars**.
**Will:** Four and a HALF?! Why not five?!
**Mei:** Hamlet is still four hours long. **Kevin the Comma**: **five stars**. Saved my grandmother.
**Kevin:** Five stars?! I don't even need my paper bag!
**Mr H:** Final quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Give **three ways** to fix the comma splice: 'The bell rang, everyone rushed out.'
**Semicolon:** Use a **full stop**, a **semicolon**, or a **conjunction** like 'and' or 'when'.
**Mr H:** Should you write 'the **childrens'** coats' or 'the **children's** coats'?
**Apostrophe:** **The children's coats** — 'children' is already plural without an 's', so add apostrophe 's'!
**Mr H:** What type of sentence is 'Although she was exhausted, Priya kept running'?
**Mei:** A **complex sentence**: a subordinate clause plus a main clause.
**Mr H:** What must always come **before** a **colon**?
**Nib:** A **complete main clause** that could stand alone as a sentence.
**Mr H:** In 'The dog wagged **its** tail', does **its** take an apostrophe?
**Kevin:** **No!** Possessive **its** never takes an apostrophe — **it's** only means 'it is' or 'it has'!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work all year, 8H. Now try the **Grammar, Punctuation & Vocabulary** quiz in your English Lab.
**Will:** All the school's a stage... and honestly? Not a bad cast.
**Mr H:** Kettle's on. Who wants tea?
